name: Politics & IR
title: Policy Analyst
blurb: Consulting clients in Japan live with Diet decisions, trade rules and geopolitics, so Arin needs to explain how policy is made and how states bargain.

chapters.title: Political systems
chapters.read: An introductory comparative-politics textbook's chapters on regime types, parliamentary vs presidential systems, federal vs unitary states, constitutions and electoral systems (plurality, proportional, mixed).
chapters.produce: Draw a one-page comparison table of Japan, the UK, the US and Germany: head of state, head of government, how the executive is chosen, federal or unitary, and electoral system.

quiz.q: In a parliamentary system, the head of government…
opts: Is chosen by, and depends on the confidence of, the legislature
Is directly elected by voters for a fixed term
Cannot be removed before the end of a fixed term
quiz.ex: Parliamentary executives come from and answer to the legislature, which can remove them by a no-confidence vote.

quiz.q: Which of these countries is a federal state?
quiz.ex: Germany divides sovereignty between the federation and its Länder; Japan and France are unitary, and the UK is unitary with devolution.

quiz.q: Single-member plurality ('first-past-the-post') elections tend to…
opts: Give each party seats exactly proportional to its votes
Produce many small parties in parliament
Favour a small number of large parties
Require a run-off in every district
quiz.ex: Winner-take-all districts punish small parties whose votes are spread thinly (Duverger's law).

quiz.q: 'Separation of powers' divides government authority mainly among…
opts: The central bank, the treasury and the stock exchange
National, regional and city governments only
Political parties, the media and interest groups
The legislature, the executive and the judiciary
quiz.ex: The classic separation is between law-making, law-executing and law-interpreting branches.

quiz.q: In a constitutional monarchy such as Japan or the UK, the monarch…
opts: Is head of state with a mainly ceremonial or symbolic role
Leads the cabinet and sets policy
Is elected by the parliament every five years
Can veto any law passed by parliament at will
quiz.ex: Political power lies with elected bodies; the monarch's role is formal and symbolic.

quiz.q: Five seats are allocated by the D'Hondt method. Votes: Party A 10,000, Party B 6,000, Party C 2,800. How many seats does Party A win?

chapters.title: Japan's parliamentary system
chapters.read: An English translation of the Constitution of Japan (Chapters I, IV and V on the Emperor, the Diet and the Cabinet) plus a textbook or House of Representatives explainer on how a bill passes the Diet (国会), the cabinet (内閣) and the two houses (衆議院・参議院).
chapters.produce: Draw a flowchart of how a cabinet bill becomes law in Japan, including what happens when the two houses disagree, with the Japanese term for each body labelled.

quiz.q: Which chamber of the National Diet can be dissolved before its term ends?
quiz.ex: Only the House of Representatives can be dissolved; the House of Councillors has fixed terms.

quiz.q: A bill passed by the House of Representatives is rejected by the House of Councillors. Under the Constitution, the House of Representatives can still make it law by passing it again with two-thirds of the members present. If 450 members are present, how many votes are needed?
quiz.ex: Two-thirds of 450 = 300 (Article 59).

quiz.q: How is Japan's Prime Minister chosen?
opts: Appointed by the Emperor at his own discretion
Designated from among Diet members by a resolution of the Diet, then formally appointed by the Emperor
quiz.ex: The Diet designates the PM (Article 67) and the Emperor performs the formal appointment (Article 6).

quiz.q: What is the Emperor's constitutional role?
opts: Head of government who chairs cabinet meetings
Holder of a veto over Diet legislation
Symbol of the State and of the unity of the people, with no powers related to government
quiz.ex: Articles 1 and 4 make the Emperor a symbol who performs only specified acts in matters of state.

quiz.q: How are members of the House of Councillors elected?
opts: For six-year terms, with half of the seats elected every three years
For four-year terms, all at once
For two-year terms, with a third elected every year
quiz.ex: Article 46 sets six-year terms with half the members elected every three years.

quiz.q: If the House of Representatives passes a no-confidence resolution against the cabinet, the cabinet must…
opts: Ask the Emperor to cancel the vote
Resign en masse, unless the House of Representatives is dissolved within ten days
Hold a national referendum within 30 days
Continue in office until the House of Councillors votes too
quiz.ex: Article 69 gives the cabinet two options: resign together or dissolve the lower house within ten days.

chapters.title: International relations theories
chapters.read: An introductory IR textbook's chapters on realism (including neorealism), liberalism (interdependence and institutions) and constructivism, plus the security dilemma and basic game theory such as the prisoner's dilemma.
chapters.produce: Take one current East Asian issue and write three short paragraphs explaining it through a realist, a liberal and a constructivist lens, ending with which explanation you find strongest and why.

quiz.q: Which assumption is central to realism?
opts: Shared identities determine all state behaviour
States act in an anarchic system where power and security come first
quiz.ex: Realists see no world government above states, so each state must look after its own security.

quiz.q: Liberal institutionalists argue that international institutions…
opts: Are irrelevant because only military power matters
Replace states as the main actors in world politics
Exist only to spread a single culture
Help states cooperate by sharing information and reducing the fear of cheating
quiz.ex: Institutions lower transaction costs and make commitments more credible, supporting cooperation.

quiz.q: The constructivist claim that 'anarchy is what states make of it' means…
opts: How states treat anarchy depends on shared ideas and identities that can change
States can abolish anarchy by signing treaties
Material power alone fixes how states behave
quiz.ex: Constructivists see interests and threats as socially constructed rather than given by structure alone.

quiz.q: Country A builds up its navy purely for defence. Country B sees this as a threat and builds up its own navy, leaving both less secure. This is an example of…
quiz.ex: Measures one state takes for its own security can reduce others' security, triggering spirals.

quiz.q: Two countries each choose to cooperate or defect. Payoffs (A, B): both cooperate 3,3; A defects while B cooperates 5,0; A cooperates while B defects 0,5; both defect 1,1. What is the Nash equilibrium?
quiz.ex: Defecting is each side's best reply whatever the other does (5 > 3 and 1 > 0), so both defect, even though both cooperating pays more.

quiz.q: A small state facing a rising great power chooses to align with that power rather than oppose it. Realists call this…
quiz.ex: Bandwagoning means joining the stronger side; balancing means aligning against it.

chapters.title: International organisations
chapters.read: The official 'about us' and founding-charter pages of the UN, WTO, IMF, ASEAN and EU, plus an IR textbook chapter on international organisations; focus on purpose, membership principles and how decisions are made.
chapters.produce: Make a one-page cheat sheet with a row per organisation (UN, WTO, IMF, ASEAN, EU): purpose, decision rule, Japan's relationship to it, and one way it could affect a consulting client.

quiz.q: Which of these countries is a permanent member of the UN Security Council?
quiz.ex: The five permanent members are China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States.

quiz.q: The WTO's most-favoured-nation (MFN) principle means a member…
opts: May set any tariff for each partner it wishes
Must give all WTO members the same trade treatment it gives its most-favoured trading partner, with limited exceptions
Must give its largest trading partner better terms than anyone else
quiz.ex: MFN is non-discrimination between trading partners; exceptions include free trade agreements.

quiz.q: What is the core role of the IMF?
opts: Lending for long-term development projects such as dams and roads
Setting the interest rates of member central banks
Monitoring members' economies and lending to countries facing balance-of-payments problems
quiz.ex: The IMF focuses on macroeconomic surveillance and balance-of-payments support; long-term project lending is the World Bank's role.

quiz.q: The 'ASEAN Way' refers to…
opts: Majority voting with binding sanctions on members
A single currency shared by all members
A supranational court whose rulings override national law
Decision-making by consultation and consensus with non-interference in members' internal affairs
quiz.ex: ASEAN stresses consensus, sovereignty and non-interference, unlike the EU's supranational model.

quiz.q: Within the EU, which institution has the main right to propose new legislation?
quiz.ex: The Commission proposes; the Parliament and the Council amend and adopt.

quiz.q: In the 'ASEAN Plus Three' framework, the three partner countries are…
opts: South Korea, Taiwan and New Zealand
quiz.ex: ASEAN Plus Three links ASEAN with China, Japan and the Republic of Korea.

chapters.title: Diplomacy and negotiation
chapters.read: A practical negotiation book's chapters on interests vs positions, BATNA, reservation points, ZOPA and anchoring, plus an IR textbook chapter on diplomacy (bilateral and multilateral, Track I and Track II, soft power).
chapters.produce: Prepare a negotiation plan for a realistic case (e.g. agreeing a part-time job's pay or a group project split): your interests, BATNA, reservation point, the other side's likely interests, and an opening anchor.

quiz.q: In negotiation, BATNA means…
opts: The best possible deal you can imagine
Your best alternative if no agreement is reached
quiz.ex: BATNA (Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement) sets the floor below which you should walk away.

quiz.q: A seller will not accept less than ¥8 million for a business. A buyer will pay at most ¥10 million. How wide is the zone of possible agreement (ZOPA)?
quiz.ex: ZOPA runs from the seller's minimum to the buyer's maximum: 10 − 8 = ¥2 million.

quiz.q: Joseph Nye's idea of 'soft power' refers to influence based on…
opts: Attraction, such as culture, values and policies others admire
quiz.ex: Soft power gets others to want what you want through attraction rather than coercion or payment.

quiz.q: 'Track II diplomacy' describes…
opts: Unofficial dialogue among academics, retired officials or civil-society groups
Formal talks between heads of government
Negotiations conducted only through the UN
Trade talks held in the second round of a WTO meeting
quiz.ex: Track I is official government diplomacy; Track II is informal and can explore ideas governments cannot yet float.

quiz.q: A negotiator opens with an ambitious first figure so later discussion centres around it. This tactic relies on…
quiz.ex: The first number tends to pull the final outcome toward it, a cognitive bias called anchoring.

quiz.q: Two parties settle a dispute by each giving way on the issue it cares less about in return for winning the issue it cares more about. This is…
quiz.ex: Trading across issues with different priorities creates joint value, the core of integrative bargaining.

chapters.title: Political economy
chapters.read: An international political economy textbook's chapters on public goods and collective action, interest groups and rent-seeking, the median voter, the main IPE traditions (liberal, mercantilist/nationalist, structuralist) and the open-economy trilemma.
chapters.produce: Write a 1-page memo on why a specific protected sector (e.g. agriculture in a country of your choice) keeps its protection, using collective action and interest-group logic.

quiz.q: Which is the best example of a pure public good?
quiz.ex: Defence is non-rival and non-excludable: protecting one person does not reduce protection for others, and no one can be shut out.

quiz.q: Mancur Olson's logic of collective action predicts that policy often favours…
opts: Small groups with concentrated benefits over large groups with diffuse costs
The largest group in society every time
Whichever group has the most moral argument
quiz.ex: Small groups organise more easily because each member gains a lot, while the many who each lose a little rarely mobilise.

quiz.q: 'Rent-seeking' means…
opts: Spending resources to obtain economic gains through political privilege rather than by creating value
Investing in research to create new products
quiz.ex: Lobbying for licences, quotas or subsidies that transfer wealth is rent-seeking.

quiz.q: Which IPE tradition sees trade surpluses and a strong domestic industrial base mainly as sources of state power?
quiz.ex: Mercantilists treat the economy as serving national power and favour exports and strategic industries.

quiz.q: The median voter theorem predicts that in a two-party, single-issue election…
opts: Both parties move to the extremes
The party with more funding always wins
Both parties move towards the position of the median voter
quiz.ex: The party closest to the median voter wins a majority, so both converge on the centre.

quiz.q: The 'impossible trinity' says a country cannot have all three at once. Japan allows free capital movement and runs its own monetary policy. What must it therefore give up?
quiz.ex: With free capital flows and independent monetary policy, the exchange rate must float, as the yen does.

boss.q: The House of Councillors receives the budget from the House of Representatives and takes no final action on it within the constitutional deadline (excluding recess). What happens?
opts: The budget lapses and must be resubmitted next year
The House of Representatives' decision becomes the decision of the Diet
The Supreme Court reviews the budget
boss.ex: Under Article 60, the lower house prevails on the budget if the upper house fails to act within 30 days or the houses cannot agree.

boss.q: A realist and a liberal institutionalist both look at the WTO. Which pairing of their views is most typical?
opts: Realist: it makes war impossible; liberal: it is irrelevant
Realist: it creates national identities; liberal: it is a military alliance
Realist: it reflects the interests of powerful states; liberal: it helps states cooperate by making cheating visible and costly
Both: it replaces states as the main actor
boss.ex: Realists see institutions as tools of power; liberals see them as reducing uncertainty and enabling cooperation.

boss.q: A country pegs its currency to the US dollar and allows capital to move freely. According to the trilemma, it has given up…
boss.ex: To hold the peg with open capital flows, its interest rates must follow those of the anchor currency.

boss.q: A UN Security Council draft resolution on a substantive matter gets 12 votes in favour, including 4 permanent members, while 1 permanent member votes against. The draft…
opts: Fails, because a permanent member voted against it
Passes, because it has more than 9 votes
Passes, because most permanent members supported it
Goes automatically to the General Assembly for a binding vote
boss.ex: A negative vote by any permanent member is a veto on substantive matters.

boss.q: How many affirmative votes, out of the 15 Security Council members, does a substantive UN Security Council resolution need at minimum (with no permanent member voting against)?
boss.ex: Article 27 of the UN Charter requires 9 affirmative votes and no veto.

boss.q: Which theory best explains Japan's strong post-war public norm against using military force abroad by pointing to identity and shared beliefs rather than material power?
boss.ex: Constructivists explain behaviour through norms and identities shaped by history and domestic debate.

boss.q: Before a tough negotiation, you secure a strong alternative offer from another party. The main effect is to…
opts: Oblige you to accept the first offer
Raise your bargaining leverage, because your walk-away option has improved
boss.ex: A better BATNA raises your reservation point and makes walking away credible.

boss.q: Rice farmers are a small share of voters, yet many rich countries protect their agriculture. Which explanation combines two ideas from this discipline?
opts: Agriculture is a pure public good
The WTO requires high farm tariffs
The median voter is always a farmer
Concentrated benefits make farmers easy to organise (collective action), and rural votes can carry extra weight in electoral systems
boss.ex: Olson's logic plus malapportionment or rural electoral weight explains why small groups win protection.

boss.q: Under Japan's Constitution, the cabinet in exercising executive power is collectively responsible to…
boss.ex: Article 66 makes the cabinet collectively responsible to the Diet, the hallmark of a parliamentary system.

boss.q: Voting power in the IMF differs from the UN General Assembly because in the IMF…
opts: Every country has exactly one equal vote
Votes are weighted mainly by each member's quota, so large economies have more say
Only the five permanent members can vote
Decisions are made only by consensus, with no votes
boss.ex: The General Assembly is one state, one vote; IMF voting power is linked to quota size.
